newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian miners says RBA gold sales "kick in pants".
newsitem.headline: Australian miners says RBA gold sales "kick in pants".

text.p: Angry Australian goldminers said on Friday a decision by the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) to sell most of its gold reserves was a "kick in the pants" for one of the country's top export earners.

The announcement of the 167-tonne sale, which helped push the gold price to a 12-year low, would shake international confidence in gold and make it more difficult to raise funds for exploration, they complained.
"It's more than disappointing...it really does impact on confidence around the world," said Acacia Resources Ltd general manager Michael Folie.
The central bank surprised the market on Thursday night by revealing it had sold more than two thirds of its holdings -- worth about US$1.8 billion at current prices -- over the past six months.

The bank argued it could generate a profit from investing the funds in other assets. And as a major gold producer, it said Australia did not benefit from holding almost 20 percent of its reserves in gold.
Delta Gold's Fiona Robertson, general manager finance, said the decision was hard to take, given government support for other industries through price support schemes and trade protection.
"For the poor old gold industry...it's just like a kick in the pants," she said. "It's showing a fundamental lack of confidence in the industry."
Mining entrepreneur and Great Central Mines chairman Joseph Gutnick said he found the RBA decision "very disappointing and astonishingly surprising".
"They should be supporting the gold industry by showing confidence in the price of gold," Gutnick said.
However, he said the impact of the sale on the gold price would prove a "short-term aberration", with strong demand for the yellow metal in Asia.
But Gutnick said he did not see the move creating problems for forward selling, a tactic used by miners to hedge against furture price drops.
Under forward selling, mines borrow gold from central banks or, less usually, commercial banks to sell before they have mined the equivalent amount as defence against falling prices.
One senior London dealer said the RBA sale would make Australian gold miners' aggressive forward selling policy more difficult to complete, forcing them to look elsewhere to borrow.
"I cannot see that as being a problem," Gutnick said.
"You can hedge in London or COMEX (New York), there is no restriction on hedging," he said.

Australian gold exports totalled A$5.7 billion in 1995/96, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, making the industry the country's second biggest export earner behind coal, excluding tourism.
But Australian miners, especially "junior miners" trying to turn around their fortunes in the outback, have already been "doing it tough".

Apart from the weak gold price -- bullion was already near four-year lows when the RBA sales were announced -- the miners have been hit by a strong Australian dollar. Those in Western Australia are also to be hit next year by a production royalty.

A recent study by Gold Fields Mineral Services Ltd reported that Australia had the highest world production costs for gold. The report put total costs at US$358 an ounce, against the roughly US$323 bullion was trading it on Friday.

Gold producers took a hammering on the Australian stock market on Friday, diving as much as 12 percent. Market leader Normandy Mining opened nearly nine percent down before recovering to close 3.4 percent down at A$1.41 (US$1.06)
